ml.headline: Mali names police commissioner Moussa Ag Infahi inspector general of security services
ml.dek: The appointment places a veteran national police officer in charge of security and civil protection services, a post Mali's Council of Ministers filled on Friday.
paragraphs: Mali's Council of Ministers appointed Police Commissioner General Moussa Ag Infahi as Inspector General of Security and Civil Protection Services at a meeting on Friday, 13 November 2026, chaired by Transition President Assimi Goïta at the Koulouba Presidential Palace. The appointment was made under the Ministry of Security and Civil Protection.

Ag Infahi, born on 20 July 1965 in Anderamboukane in Ménaka region, has spent decades in public security, investigation and security sector reform. His career includes posts in police stations, the national police's general directorate, investigation units and international cooperation. He trained at the National School of Administration (ENA) and, from February to September 1996, at the special platoon of the Inter-Armed Forces Military School (EMIA) in Koulikoro.
The same day, a decree signed by Goïta named Mouhamed B. Diarra director general of the National Institute of Social Security (INPS), succeeding Idrissa Bakary Diarra.

mr.headline: Mauritania reclassifies bloggers' case as terrorism
mr.dek: What began as accusations of financial blackmail has shifted three times in seven weeks, now landing with anti-terrorism investigators.
paragraphs: Mauritanian authorities have reclassified the case of several bloggers, known as the "bloggers from abroad," as a terrorism investigation. This marks the third qualification change for the affair in less than seven weeks. The case began on September 30 with a government announcement of a "financial blackmail network," then shifted on October 7 to "financial corruption and moral depravity." On November 13, the investigation was assigned to the unit handling terrorism crimes.

The investigation now involves seven individuals detained, nine under judicial supervision, and arrest warrants for seven others, many of whom are abroad. The case originated from Facebook pages managed by Mauritanian bloggers, primarily residing in the United States, who have been publishing critical content since 2018. Prominent figures like Sidi Ould Kmache, Al-Hafiz Ould Loubad, and Diaa Al-Haq Ould Abih are among those sought by the authorities.

The prosecution has framed the legal basis for the case around three axes: criticism of political figures, intrusion into the private lives of officials including the president and his family, and the publication of sensitive military information. These allegations, which evolved from online posts and payment app transfers, have led to the case being transferred from the State Security Directorate to the anti-terrorism investigation unit.

mr.headline: UK pledges to implement export credit deal with Mauritania

paragraphs: Guy Harrison, the United Kingdom's ambassador to Mauritania, said his country is committed to implementing a memorandum of understanding signed with Mauritania on export credit. He made the remarks at a reception the embassy held in Nouakchott on Friday to mark the British sovereign's birthday.

Harrison said the deal will expand bilateral cooperation in financing infrastructure projects and open investment and partnership opportunities for economic actors in both countries. He said the embassy in Nouakchott continues to work on strengthening trade and investment ties.

Harrison praised British firms operating in Mauritania, naming BP, Chariot Energy and Ora Energy. He also reaffirmed the UK's commitment to cooperation on climate resilience, food security and protecting livelihoods, which he called essential to the country's stability.

mr.headline: Mauritania media authority lists professional outlets
mr.dek: The High Authority for Press and Audiovisual releases a preliminary list of national media outlets meeting professional standards.
paragraphs: The High Authority for Press and Audiovisual (HAPA) of Mauritania published a preliminary list on Friday of national media outlets that satisfactorily meet the professional and institutional standards required by law. Several audiovisual outlets, including Al-Sahel, Sahara 24, Al-Mourabitoun, Al-Medina, and Chinguetti, were identified as compliant.

For online media, HAPA identified the press agency Sahara Média, the Al-Sakhra Centre, Takadoumi, Mauritanie Aujourd’hui, Belwar Média, Tawater, Al-Murasiloun, Madar, the Mauritanian press agency, Cridem, Nouakchott Direct, Libjawi, Kader, Al-Tayyar, Info Plus, Mauritanie Aujourd’hui, Al-Fikr, Al-Chourouk Media, Mauritania News, Tahaad, and Al-Muraqib. The written press list included Elilam Media Groupe, Al-Amal, La Voix des Ouvriers, Le Rénovateur, the Al-Sada group for media, Authentique, Le Quotidien de Nouakchott, Éveil Hebdo, and FOOYRE BAMTAAARE.

HAPA stated that this decision was based on a technical evaluation from an exhaustive investigation into the national journalistic landscape in 2026, along with reliability audit reports and performance evaluations of national audiovisual institutions from 2025-2026. Further technical evaluations of internet site content and a report from the professional journalists' registry also informed the list.

mu.headline: Reform Party leader warns Mauritius rate rise will squeeze household budgets
mu.dek: Roshi Bhadain says the central bank's hike from 4.75% to 5% will add to borrowing costs as inflation reached 6.4% last month.
paragraphs: The Monetary Policy Committee raised the key interest rate from 4.75% to 5% in the course of this week to contain inflation, which reached 6.4% last month, according to the bank's announcement.

Roshi Bhadain, leader of the Reform Party, said in a video posted on Friday to his Facebook page that the increase would raise the repayments of households with bank loans or credit purchases. Citing figures he attributes to Statistics Mauritius, he said household debt already exceeded Rs 220 billion in September 2026, and that one household in two is in debt.

He also argued that the previous increase, from 4.50% to 4.75% in May, did not produce the expected results, and that the new rise will not solve the inflation problem. He said the decision should not have been taken at this stage.

mz.headline: Mozambique mining titles yield no operations
mz.dek: Hundreds of mining concessions and certificates have not begun operations, with many inactive for over a decade.
paragraphs: Mozambique holds 169 mining concessions and 371 small-scale mining certificates where operations have not commenced, according to the Administrative Court's 2025 State General Account.
Of these inactive titles, 67 concessions and 72 certificates have remained dormant for more than 10 years, with the court finding no evidence of government-approved extensions for these delays.

The court recommended stricter oversight of licence holders' financial capacity and development progress, following the introduction of a new Mining Law in 2026 designed to enforce development timelines.

mz.headline: Sovereign fund watchdog says it was shut out of key policy work
mz.dek: Mozambique's Supervisory Committee of the Sovereign Fund says the Finance Ministry was slow to share information and left it out of drafting the Investment Policy.
paragraphs: The Supervisory Committee of Mozambique's Sovereign Fund, an independent body that monitors revenues from the Rovuma natural gas project, says it was excluded from drafting the fund's management instruments. It also says it has not received the fund's annual financial report.

The complaints appear in the committee's first-quarter 2026 report, sent to Parliament, and were cited by the Plan and Budget Commission while reviewing the fund's 2025 accounts. The report also points to the absence of independent validation of projections, external audit and an independent expert, and to the unpublished management agreement with the Bank of Mozambique, signed on 19 November 2025.

The committee described revenue management as reasonable and said there was no breach of the law or regulations, despite organisational problems. It has recommended revising the law creating the fund and its regulations, to extend its oversight to projects financed from gas revenues.

mz.headline: Mozambique Supreme Court trial uses new audio-visual recording
mz.dek: The Supreme Court in Maputo will begin the trial of Venâncio Mondlane on Tuesday, November 17, using new technology to record hearings.
paragraphs: The Supreme Court in Maputo will begin the trial of Venâncio Mondlane on Tuesday, November 17, using new audio and video recording technology for hearings. This system, which transcribes recordings into written documents, aims to significantly reduce trial length, according to Supreme Court judge-counsellor Pedro Nhatitima. The trial will take place in the criminal section of the Supreme Court, with daily sessions scheduled from 10:00 to 15:30 local time.

The case involves charges brought by the Public Prosecutor’s Office against Mondlane, a former presidential candidate who has not recognized the election results. The proceedings relate to post-election demonstrations between October 2024 and March 2025, during which over 400 people died in clashes with police and hundreds of businesses were vandalized. Mondlane faces charges including public glorification of crime and incitement to terrorism. The trial will hear from 12 prosecution witnesses, 20 defence witnesses, and two experts from mobile operators Vodacom and Tmcel.

The courtroom has a maximum capacity of 45 people and will include five Supreme Court judge-counsellors, two deputy attorneys-general, and legal representatives. Mondlane is standing trial before the Supreme Court because he is a member of the Council of State, which lifted his immunity.

mz.headline: Mozambican boy, 15, found brutally murdered
mz.dek: His 12-year-old friend remains missing after they disappeared from a Sant'Egidio Community program.
paragraphs: A 15-year-old boy, Juvêncio, was found dead with extreme signs of violence in the Matola River on Monday, November 9. He and his 12-year-old friend, Ilton, had disappeared on Saturday, November 7, after attending a Sant’Egidio Community program in Matola. Fishermen discovered Juvêncio’s body, which showed clear evidence of brutality.

Father Rolando Curzi, a priest with the Sant’Egidio Community, stated that the nature of the mutilations suggests the crime may be linked to magical-superstitious practices. Ilton is still missing, and the search continues in Matola. The Sant’Egidio Community is urging authorities to investigate the swift murder of the young peace advocate.

This is the first such case involving children attending the Community’s centre, though similar incidents have occurred involving minors, particularly boys with albinism. The Sant’Egidio Community runs a BRAVO! program for the civil registration of children to provide protection. Their Matola Nutrition Centre feeds about 500 disadvantaged minors weekly and offers educational support to over 100 on Saturdays.

na.headline: Namibia's pension fund has N$5.1 billion ready for projects
na.dek: The Government Institutions Pension Fund (GIPF) has committed N$28.2 billion to unlisted investments, with N$23.1 billion already invested.
paragraphs: The Government Institutions Pension Fund (GIPF) has N$5.1 billion still available for investment in suitable Namibian projects, even as the country grapples with unemployment, a housing crisis and infrastructure gaps. Board chairperson Penda Ithindi disclosed the figures at the recent GIPF Investment Symposium.

Ithindi said the fund will not compromise its investment principles: projects must be financially viable, properly governed and sufficiently secured. He said the money belongs to thousands of Namibian pension contributors and cannot be spent to satisfy political promises.

The commentary calls for a dedicated national project preparation facility, bringing together the ministry of finance, the National Planning Commission, development finance institutions, local authorities and private-sector experts. It would identify viable projects, prepare business cases and secure approvals, with housing and urban infrastructure named as priorities.

na.headline: Namibia signs N$174m contract for Windhoek hospital site
na.dek: Elderwood Trading CC and Shangsheng Construction will prepare the Havana site for the capital's first district hospital within 12 months.
paragraphs: The construction of Windhoek's first district hospital has moved forward with a N$174 million contract signed for site preparation. Elderwood Trading CC, in joint venture with Shangsheng Construction, will undertake bulk earthworks and install essential infrastructure services over 12 months at the Havana site. The contract covers access roads, stormwater drainage, water supply, sewerage networks, and electricity services.

Penda Ithindi, executive director for the ministry of health and social services, called the contract signing a historic milestone for Namibia's healthcare sector. He noted that Windhoek's population now exceeds half a million, making new healthcare infrastructure urgent. The new facility aims to ease pressure on Windhoek Central Hospital and Katutura Intermediate Hospital, allowing them to focus on specialised care.

Idi Itope, chief executive officer of the Central Procurement Board of Namibia (CPBN), stated that the N$174 million investment must translate into tangible development. He urged the contractor to adhere to the 12-month implementation period and maintain quality standards. The CPBN oversees the contract, which is the first phase of the hospital development, with hospital building construction to follow.

na.headline: Swakopmund wall collapse kills casual worker at rest camp
na.dek: Stephanus Hamutenya died after a section of a concrete wall fell on him during demolition work at the Municipal Rest Camp in Swakopmund.
paragraphs: Stephanus Hamutenya, a casual worker engaged by the contractor Frampton Investment CC, was fatally injured on Wednesday, 11 November 2026, when a concrete wall collapsed on him at the Municipal Rest Camp in Swakopmund. He was working with other employees on the demolition of existing bungalows at the Fish Bungalows site when the wall fell unexpectedly.

Fellow workers pulled him from the rubble and emergency medical services attended to him before taking him to hospital, where he died of his injuries. The Municipality of Swakopmund confirmed the death in a media statement, extending condolences to his family, friends and colleagues.

All construction and demolition activities at the site have been temporarily suspended while investigations and safety assessments are carried out. The municipality said it is working with the contractor and the relevant authorities to establish the full circumstances of the incident.

na.headline: Namibia faces power, regulation hurdles for mineral processing
na.dek: Former central bank governor Johannes !Gawaxab identified electricity costs and unpredictable rules as key barriers to developing Namibia's mineral sector.
paragraphs: Namibia's mineral beneficiation plans face significant obstacles, including high electricity costs and uncertain regulations, according to former Bank of Namibia Governor Johannes !Gawaxab. Speaking in Johannesburg, !Gawaxab stated that resource-rich African nations struggle to translate mineral wealth into industrial development due to structural barriers. He highlighted electricity, regulatory frameworks, infrastructure, and access to patient capital as the primary constraints.

"Africa has an electrons problem, a rules problem, a competitiveness, and a patient-capital problem," !Gawaxab said, emphasizing that value addition requires solving these issues. He noted that while Namibia has imposed export restrictions on minerals like lithium and cobalt since 2023 to encourage domestic processing, these measures alone are insufficient. "Bans tell capital where it may not go. They don’t tell it where it should go," he explained.

For Namibia's mineral processing ambitions to succeed, electricity must be competitive with international prices, and reliable power is essential for smelting and refining. !Gawaxab also stressed that investors need predictable, long-term rules, not ones that frequently change. He suggested that African institutional investors, such as pension funds, could increase their role in financing mineral processing and infrastructure projects.

na.headline: Namibian artists urged to master direct licensing
na.dek: Nascam handles only certain royalties, leaving artists to exploit other rights such as synchronisation and master use licences on their own.
paragraphs: Many Namibian musicians believe that registering with the collective management organisation Nascam means their copyright administration is taken care of. The source says this is a myth: Nascam issues blanket licences to broadcasters, pubs, shopping malls and live venues, deducts administration costs, and distributes the rest to members.

Rights outside that blanket scheme must be handled by the copyright holder. The most lucrative is the synchronisation licence, which a filmmaker, television producer or advertising agency needs before pairing music with moving images. No collecting society in Namibia administers sync rights on a blanket basis, so the fee depends on market value, length of use, territory and project budget.

Sync licences cover only the song itself, so a company using a studio recording needs a separate master use licence, which artists who fully own their masters can charge for alongside the sync fee. Under the 1994 Copyright and Neighbouring Rights Protection Act, using a track in a corporate video without clearing the master is direct infringement, and anyone wishing to sample a recording must negotiate a clearance fee, usually an upfront buyout or a co-publishing split.

ne.headline: Attack near Téra in Niger's Tillabéri region kills at least 37, sources say
ne.dek: Local sources told AFP the attack took place near Téra, close to the borders with Burkina Faso and Mali.
paragraphs: An attack took place on Thursday, November 12, in the Tillabéri region of western Niger, an area that has been the epicentre of terrorist violence. It happened near the locality of Téra, close to the borders with Burkina Faso and Mali.
Local sources cited by the Agence France-Presse news agency put the death toll at at least 37. Niger's authorities have not issued any official statement or death toll so far.
The figure has not been confirmed by officials, and no further details about the attackers or the victims were reported.

ne.headline: Niger bans all peanut exports to build local oil processing
ne.dek: Customs officers and security forces may seize any peanuts caught leaving the country, and the state keeps them.
paragraphs: Niger's Minister of Commerce and Industry, Abdoulaye Seydou, announced at a press briefing on Friday 13 November 2026 that peanut exports are banned across the whole country under decree 05-18, dated 11 November 2026. The aim, he said, is to strengthen the processing and consumption of local peanut products, especially oil.

The minister said Niger imports cooking oil from distant countries even though it has the raw material to produce enough good-quality oil from peanuts at home. The ban adds to existing bans on exports of millet, polished rice, paddy and sorghum. Exceptional export permits may be granted to countries of the AES confederation under a set procedure.

Ministry of Commerce inspectors, customs agents and the defence and security forces are authorised to enforce the ban. Any peanuts found in an attempted export will be seized systematically and handed to the state through the usual judicial procedure.

ne.headline: World Bank pledges $700 million more for Niger over five years
ne.dek: The new partnership strategy, launched by Niger's finance minister, is meant to create more and better jobs, especially for young people and women.
paragraphs: Niger's President, General Abdourahamane Tiani, received Ousmane Diagana, the World Bank's vice-president for West and Central Africa, in Niamey on Friday, 13 November, leading a large delegation. The talks covered the Kandadji Programme, a new partnership framework between the Nigerien state and the bank, agriculture and energy.

Diagana acknowledged that implementation of the Kandadji Project had been delayed for various reasons. A round-table with all partners, held on 11 November under the prime minister's leadership, produced agreements that he said should allow the project to restart quickly. He said the bank would mobilise about $700 million in additional public-sector resources during the strategy, on top of a portfolio of more than $4 billion already in Niger.

The five-year strategy is to fund structural programmes, including a major bank-backed scheme that gives young people access to credit to start small and medium enterprises. Diagana said electricity, agriculture and water were the three sectors that matter most for development, and cited the Mission 300 electricity initiative.

ne.headline: Niger hands solar equipment worth 86 million FCFA to Poudrière hospital
ne.dek: The energy and health ministries say uninterrupted power protects mothers and newborns at the Niamey regional hospital, which treats hundreds of patients daily.
paragraphs: Niger's Minister of Energy, Colonel Seyni Alzouma, handed solar power equipment worth about 86 million FCFA to his health counterpart, Colonel Major Garba Hakimi, on Friday, 12 November 2026. The equipment, financed by Istithmar West Africa, is for the Poudrière Regional Hospital in Niamey.

Alzouma said electricity is a basic condition for safe care in a hospital, especially in maternity and operating theatres. He listed the functions it supports: biomedical equipment, lighting in delivery and operating rooms, the storage of vaccines and medicines, and emergency treatment.

The hospital receives several hundred patients a day, mainly in gynaecology and paediatrics. Alzouma said the government plans to electrify 80% of health centres by 2030 to cope with power cuts and the high cost of running generators.

rw.headline: Rwanda pilots centralised school meals
rw.dek: A new system prepares food in a central kitchen and delivers it to 266 teachers and 15,014 students across five schools.
paragraphs: The Rwandan government has started a pilot programme for centralised school meals, preparing food in bulk and delivering it to schools, a method similar to systems in Japan and South Korea. The education ministry says the shift is also aimed at reducing reliance on firewood, improving nutrition and lowering the cost of school feeding. The pilot launched on Friday and serves 15,014 students and 266 teachers across five public schools in Rwamagana District.

Meals are cooked at a central kitchen at GS Bujyujyu in Muyumbu Sector and transported to the schools in electric vehicles, so each school no longer has to cook its own food. The facility was inaugurated on Friday, November 13, by Minister of State for Education Claudette Irere, alongside representatives of Solid'Africa, the local social enterprise implementing the project.

The arrangement follows a hub-and-spoke model also used in Japan, where municipal school lunch centres, known as kyushoku centres, prepare meals for several schools. Japan runs this system alongside school-based kitchens as part of a nationwide school feeding programme.

rw.headline: Rwanda seeks $3.05bn from investors for power grid and climate projects
rw.dek: The government is pitching its electricity and urban resilience needs to international lenders at the COP31 climate conference.
paragraphs: Rwanda is seeking US$3.05 billion in international investment for its electricity ambitions, including US$1.3 billion for grid infrastructure. Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva presented the country's priorities at the COP31 climate conference, where Rwanda called for stronger partnerships with multilateral development banks and development finance institutions.

On November 12 Nsengiyumva attended a high-level event on the Global Grids Accelerator, presided over by United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres. Rwanda said it needs to expand transmission capacity by 70 per cent and raise regional electricity trade from 100 megawatts to 200 megawatts.

The country also highlighted renewable energy, clean cooking, electric mobility, sustainable agriculture and the circular economy. The discussions included the Mission 300 initiative, which aims to connect 300 million people in Africa to electricity by 2030.

rw.headline: Mali beats Rwanda 3-2 in Bamako after Amavubi twice led
rw.dek: Mamadou Camara headed in the winner six minutes from time, ending Rwanda's unbeaten start in Group K of 2027 AFCON qualifying.
paragraphs: Mali came from behind twice to beat Rwanda 3-2 in Bamako on Friday, November 13, in the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifier. Amavubi had taken the lead through Jojea Kwizera in the 28th minute and again through Phanuel Kavita, who rose above the Mali defenders to head home a corner in the 53rd minute.

Mali restored parity before halftime in the 42nd minute. Substitute Mamadou Camara then headed in a corner six minutes from time at Stade du 26 Mars, giving the hosts all three points. Rwanda lost for the first time in Group K.
The defeat ended Rwanda's perfect start to the campaign.

rw.headline: Kagame begins Cambodia state visit with royal welcome
rw.dek: Rwanda's president was received by Cambodia's King Norodom Sihamoni in Phnom Penh before a week of talks and signings.
paragraphs: Rwandan President Paul Kagame and First Lady Jeannette Kagame were received by Cambodia's King Norodom Sihamoni at the Royal Palace in Phnom Penh on Friday, 13 November, in a formal welcome that opened the state visit. A private audience between the King and Rwanda's leader followed the ceremony.

Cambodia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs says the trip will bring talks with the country's senior leaders, and agreements on trade, investment, aviation and tourism are due to be signed. Kagame is scheduled to meet Senate President Hun Sen, National Assembly President Khuon Sudary and Prime Minister Hun Manet, and is also expected to visit the Independence Monument.

After the visit, Kagame will attend the 20th Summit of the International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF) in Phnom Penh on 15 and 16 November. Rwanda's Secretary-General, Louise Mushikiwabo, is seeking another term there, against three challengers, in a vote on 16 November.

rw.headline: Foreign ministers gather in Phnom Penh to prepare Francophonie summit texts
rw.dek: Ministers will finalise the Phnom Penh Declaration and a peacebuilding resolution before heads of state meet at the 20th Francophonie Summit.
paragraphs: Foreign ministers and government representatives from member states of La Francophonie, the International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF), will hold the 48th Ministerial Conference on November 14 at the Sokha Phnom Penh Hotel in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. Rwanda is among the countries taking part. The organisers say the meeting prepares recommendations for heads of state and government attending the 20th Francophonie Summit.

Ministers were due to finalise core texts for summit adoption, including the Phnom Penh Declaration, a resolution on peacebuilding and crisis resolution, and the Phnom Penh Appeal on cultural heritage and diversity. The conference will also hear candidate presentations for the OIF Secretary-General, followed by closed-door deliberations, and review institutional and financial governance.

The debate centres on the theme "Reinvesting in Peace for Shared Prosperity and Sustainable Stability". Ministers will also coordinate economic initiatives alongside FrancoTech 2026, which covers AI, digital governance, fintech and food security, and the Francophone Entrepreneurs Forum.

st.headline: President names ADI leader Américo Ramos prime minister
st.dek: Carlos Vila Nova chose Ramos after the MLSTP, which won the most seats, could not show it had enough parliamentary support to govern.
paragraphs: President Carlos Vila Nova has appointed Américo Ramos, leader of the ADI party, as Prime Minister and Head of Government of São Tomé and Príncipe, according to Presidential Decree No. 32/2026, which the presidency made public on Thursday. The appointment followed a 24-hour deadline the president had set for ADI to name a prime minister.

The presidency said the MLSTP, the most-voted party, had not provided the elements needed for political stability and governability. ADI, which won 23 seats in the 27 September legislative elections, signed a parliamentary agreement with the MCI-PUN, led by António Monteiro and holding six seats, giving them a combined 29 deputies. The MLSTP, with 24 seats but no absolute majority, had urged the president to reject an ADI-led government.
The Movimento BASTA criticised the decision and called for a government of national unity, arguing the appointment rests only on guarantees of parliamentary support.

st.headline: MLSTP fails to form government after election win
st.dek: The ADI party, which finished second, secured a 29-seat majority with the MCI-PS/PUN coalition, and its leader Américo d'Oliveira dos Ramos was named Prime Minister on November 12.
paragraphs: The Movimento de Libertação de São Tomé e Príncipe (MLSTP) failed to form a government despite winning the most seats in the September 27 legislative elections. The party secured 24 deputies, while the ADI party won 23 seats, and the MCI-PS/PUN coalition took 6. The MLSTP's inability to consolidate its victory led to its exclusion from governing.

While the MLSTP celebrated its narrow win, the ADI party formed a stable parliamentary majority of 29 deputies by agreeing with the MCI-PS/PUN coalition. President Carlos Vila Nova, after consulting political parties, gave the MLSTP 30 days to form a government, a deadline they could not meet. Consequently, the President invited the ADI to present a candidate for Prime Minister.

On November 12, 2026, Dr. Américo d’Oliveira dos Ramos was appointed Prime Minister, leading the ADI party. The MLSTP also lost leadership positions in the National Assembly to the ADI and MCI-PS/PUN. Political analysts suggest the MLSTP leader should consider stepping down and calling an extraordinary congress to elect new leadership to avoid further political isolation.

sn.headline: Senegal budget rejection blocks $2.2 billion IMF loan
sn.dek: The National Assembly's finance commission rejected budget proposals, halting progress on a critical IMF loan.
paragraphs: Senegal's 2027 budget remains blocked after the National Assembly's finance commission rejected proposals from various ministries and state revenues on Saturday. The ruling Pastef party cited a "lack of budgetary sincerity" for the rejections.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on November 12 reiterated that adopting a budget is essential for Senegal to access a $2.2 billion loan program. The country faces a complicated financial situation, with this blockage impacting its ability to secure vital funding.
Abdou Lahad Ndiaye, the Minister of Land and Air Transport, publicly reacted to the rejection of his ministry's 2027 budget project by the finance commission.

sn.headline: Thiès destroys 48 tonnes of unsafe goods seized in six months
sn.dek: Officials burned the stock by incineration, with the seized goods valued at 26 million CFA francs.
paragraphs: Over six months, the regional commerce service in Thiès seized 48.306 tonnes of products unfit for consumption, and officials had them incinerated on Friday, November 13, 2026. The stock was valued at about 26 million CFA francs.

The ceremony was presided over by Ababacar Sadikh Niang, the deputy governor in charge of development, who said food products made up 80% of the stock, insecticides 10%, and pharmaceuticals, cosmetics and hardware the remaining 10%. He called on residents to stay vigilant about using such products and to report suspicious goods to the competent services.

The destroyed goods included 42 tonnes of food such as drinks, biscuits, milk and mustard, along with 5.306 tonnes of counterfeit insecticides. The operation was carried out by the fire brigade in the presence of the gendarmerie company commander and consumer association representatives.

sn.headline: Senegal president attends Francophonie summit in Cambodia
sn.dek: President Bassirou Diomaye Faye arrived in Phnom Penh on November 13, 2026, for the 20th Francophonie Summit.
paragraphs: President Bassirou Diomaye Faye arrived in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, on Friday, November 13, 2026, to participate in the 20th Summit of Heads of State and Government of the Francophonie. The summit is held under the theme: “Reinvesting in Peace for Shared Prosperity and Lasting Stability.” This meeting is particularly historic as Senegal and Cambodia are among the four founding members of the institutional Francophonie, established in Niamey, Niger, in 1970.

The summit brings together nations to define new directions for the Francophone space amidst international geopolitical tensions and conflicts. Discussions are expected to focus on strengthening dialogue, consolidating peace, and promoting shared prosperity. Senegal's participation continues its diplomatic commitment to peace and multilateral dialogue, following its involvement in the Paris Peace Forum.

President Faye will engage in discussions on the future of the Francophonie and collective responses to contemporary challenges. The summit marks a reunion of founding nations 56 years after the organization's inception, aiming to contribute to global stability and cooperation.

sn.headline: Dakar hosts breaking finals at Youth Olympic Games
sn.dek: 12 breakers aged 14 to 17, from around the world, fought duels on November 12 to qualify for the finals.
paragraphs: Breaking, also called break dance, returned to the Olympic programme at the Youth Olympic Games (JOJ 2026) in Dakar, four years after the Paris 2024 Games. On November 12, 12 breakers aged 14 to 17, from countries around the world, competed in fast head-to-head duels to qualify for the final.

Crowds in Dakar turned out for the contest, drawn to the acrobatic style. The discipline is not on the programme for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics, which makes its place in Dakar a rare chance for young dancers to compete at this level.

Aminata Touré, the High Representative of President Bassirou Diomaye Faye, congratulated the president on the success of the Games in a social media post and praised Senegalese hospitality, known as Téranga.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone charcoal burning causes deforestation
sl.dek: The practice of burning wood for charcoal is depleting forests and threatening food security in Sierra Leone.
paragraphs: Pa Alimamy, a 65-year-old charcoal burner in Sierra Leone, relies on the trade for his family's livelihood, a common practice in Freetown and other towns due to limited access to electricity and clean cooking options. The National Energy Compact states only 36% of the population has electricity access, and 15% has clean cooking access.

Charcoal production involves cutting down trees, including economic ones like mango and orange, leading to deforestation, habitat loss, and environmental degradation. Paul Lamin from the Environmental Protection Agency acknowledged the hazards, noting that treeless land is exposed to climate change effects and threatening food security.

The burning process emits greenhouse gases, contributing to climate change and air pollution, with traditional wood energy emitting 2.4 GT of carbon dioxide equivalent annually. The Food and Agricultural Organization (FAO) warns that continued unsustainable charcoal production will exacerbate climate change, potentially reducing future wood-energy supplies.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone seeks stronger coordination of national data systems
sl.dek: A national review found more than 70 data initiatives in Sierra Leone, yet only about 30% of national data systems exchange information effectively.
paragraphs: The Ministry of Planning and Economic Development (MoPED) is seeking stronger coordination among government institutions to improve Sierra Leone's national data systems, after concerns over fragmented platforms, limited information sharing and weak investment in data management. The issue was discussed on November 13, 2026, at the inaugural Steering Committee meeting of the Power of Data (PoD) Initiative in the MoPED Conference Hall in Freetown.

A national review presented at the meeting identified more than 70 data initiatives, about 160 stakeholders, over 20 policy and legal frameworks and 10 development partners. Less than 1% of the national budget went to data and statistics, and the country's data protection legislation remains at draft stage. Deputy Development Secretary I, Usman Cherry Conteh, urged government agencies to work together to prevent duplication and produce practical results.

The Minister's statement, read by Conteh, called for existing data platforms to be connected rather than replaced, and recommended an implementation plan with clear responsibilities, timelines, budget allocations and monitoring arrangements. UNFPA Deputy Representative Sibeso Mululuma encouraged the government to increase domestic financing, and Power of Data consultant Bailah Molleh outlined five priority areas under the proposed 2026–2030 Country Implementation Framework.

sl.headline: Orange Sierra Leone holds talks with government on network expansion
sl.dek: The company's board chairman and chief executive met the speaker of parliament, the chief minister and the telecoms regulator's director general on Thursday, November 12.
paragraphs: Orange Sierra Leone has held talks with senior government officials on improving telecommunications services, expanding network coverage and increasing investment in digital infrastructure. The meetings on Thursday, November 12, brought together the company's board chairman, Brelotte Ba, and its chief executive, Aicha Touré, with representatives of key government institutions.

The delegation met Speaker of Parliament Segepoh Solomon Thomas, Chief Minister David Moinina Sengeh, National Telecommunications Authority (NatCA) Director General Amara Brewah and Minister of Communication, Technology and Innovation Salamata Momonah Bah. Key issues discussed included extending coverage to more communities, improving service reliability and strengthening consumer protection.

The company said it would keep working with government institutions and regulators on innovation, connectivity and digital and economic development. A separate report of the same engagements said Ba and Touré also paid a courtesy visit to President Julius Maada Bio at State House in Freetown, where they reaffirmed the group's investment commitment.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone vice presidents rarely become president
sl.dek: No vice president in Sierra Leone has ever been elected president, raising questions about the current vice president's future.
paragraphs: The office of Vice President in Sierra Leone has historically been a political dead end, with no holder ever ascending to the presidency. Since independence, vice presidents have often been appointed to balance political considerations rather than to groom successors.

Past vice presidents like Sorie Ibrahim Koroma and Francis Minah under Siaka Stevens were powerful but not groomed for succession, with Minah facing execution after an alleged coup. Solomon Ekuma Berewa, considered well-prepared, lost the 2007 presidential election despite his experience, indicating that competence alone is insufficient for electoral success.

Samuel Sam-Sumana's experience as a vice president who was later estranged from the president, expelled from his party, and left politically isolated, further illustrates the precariousness of the position. Victor Bockarie Foh's short tenure also lacked succession ambition.

so.headline: Al-Shabaab ambush kills eight near Kenya-Somalia border
so.dek: Attackers blocked a road in Mandera County and fired on a vehicle carrying police reservists and construction workers to work.
paragraphs: Eight people, including two police reservists, five construction workers and a driver, were killed on Tuesday when suspected Al-Shabaab militants ambushed a vehicle in northeast Kenya. Mandera County Police Commander Robinson Ndiwa said the attack happened at about 7 a.m. in Hagarsu, on the Mandera-Arabia-Fino-Lafey-Elwak road near the Somali border.

Residents saw heavily armed assailants block the road before opening fire on the vehicle, Ndiwa said. He said the motive had not yet been established, and that combined security agencies were pursuing the attackers, who retreated into nearby thickets.

The area recorded its worst terror attack on December 2, 2014, when 36 quarry miners were killed in their tents. In December 2019, militants used improvised explosive devices to destroy road construction machinery at Hagarsu Bida, valued at Sh39.8 million.

so.headline: UN experts call Somalia's chief justice dismissal a blatant interference
so.dek: United Nations experts say the dismissal of Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed breaches the independence of Somalia's judiciary and back the Supreme Court's ruling against it.
paragraphs: United Nations independent experts have condemned President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's abrupt dismissal of Somalia's Chief Justice, Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, as a "blatant interference with the independence of the judiciary." In a statement issued on 12 November, the rapporteurs on judicial independence and on human rights and counter-terrorism said the presidential decree of 4 November was a deliberate circumvention of constitutional safeguards, issued the night before the Supreme Court was to rule on extending presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years.

No proposal was sought from the Judicial Services Commission and parliamentary approval was not obtained. Three days later a replacement chief justice was sworn in at a ceremony attended by the President, an act the experts said further eroded the rule of law. The experts also called for the immediate restoration of protection for seven judges whose personal security was withdrawn despite acknowledged threats, and for security forces to be pulled back from the Supreme Court.

On 5 November, five Supreme Court judges ruled the term extensions unlawful, declared the mandates of the President and Parliament expired and ordered elections within 90 days. The same bench found the removal of Chief Justice Ahmed unconstitutional. The government refused to comply, and the experts warned that irregular reform and a weak judiciary risk undermining Somalia's fight against Al-Shabaab.

so.headline: US troops leave Somalia's Baledogle airfield
so.dek: Runway repair costs of tens of millions of dollars prompted the US Africa Command to withdraw personnel.
paragraphs: United States troops have withdrawn from Baledogle Military Airfield in southern Somalia due to the deteriorating condition of the runway, which had become unsafe for aircraft. Army Lieutenant General John Brennan, deputy commander of US Africa Command (AFRICOM), stated that the decision was purely economic, with most personnel relocated to Mogadishu. Resurfacing the runway would have cost tens of millions of dollars, Brennan told reporters.

Baledogle, located about 90-100 kilometres northwest of Mogadishu in the Lower Shabelle region, has served as a major hub for US counter-terrorism operations and training of Somalia’s Danab special forces since around 2012. The base experienced a large Al-Shabaab assault in September 2019. Despite risks, the US Navy awarded a contract of over $12 million for emergency runway repairs in 2018, and a new medical facility was announced in May 2025.

AFRICOM stated that the departure does not signify a reduction in American support for Somali security forces fighting Al-Shabaab, with US airstrikes continuing. Officials indicated a possible return to the airfield if conditions change, though no firm plans exist. Ugandan and Somali forces reportedly remain at the site. The US previously ordered nearly 700 personnel out in late 2020, with hundreds returning in 2022.

so.headline: Turkey denies plans to send 15,000 troops to Somalia
so.dek: Ankara says its existing forces will keep to training and advisory work after Uganda began pulling its own troops out.
paragraphs: Turkey has denied reports that it plans to send 15,000 troops to Somalia, saying the claims do not reflect the truth. Ministry of National Defense spokesperson Rear Admiral Zeki Aktürk said on Thursday that Turkish forces already in the country would continue their training and advisory mission.

Aktürk said the Somalia-Turkish Task Force and the Air Element Command were helping to build Somalia's counter-terrorism capacity through military assistance, training and advisory activities. The figure first appeared in early November in Somali media, which cited unnamed security sources and claimed Turkey had agreed to deploy soldiers to Barawe, Baidoa and Mogadishu before January 2027.

Uganda has begun withdrawing its forces from Somalia after nearly 20 years, with all Ugandan personnel due to leave by the end of 2027. Turkey's main base is Camp TURKSOM in Mogadishu, opened in 2017, and its mandate in the country has been extended through July 2028.

ss.headline: South Sudan's electoral commission moves December vote to February 2027
ss.dek: The National Elections Commission has pushed polling day to February 11, 2027, nearly two months past the December 2026 deadline set in law.
paragraphs: South Sudan's National Elections Commission (NEC) has set February 11, 2027, as the new polling day for the country's general elections, replacing December 22, 2026. The revised calendar, issued by the commission, moves the whole electoral timetable back by nearly two months.

Radio Tamazuj reports that the timetable raises questions about compliance with the National Elections Act, which requires the voter register to be published at least three months before elections. Voter registration runs from November 14 to November 28, with the provisional register due on November 29 and final publication on January 10, 2027.

The campaign period is set to run for 45 days, from December 27 to February 9, 2027, with February 10 as a campaign-free day. Candidate lists are due to be published on January 18, 2027. The timetable also allows 148 days for resolving election disputes, from February 17 to July 15, 2027.

ss.headline: South Sudan Bar Association to sue Interior Ministry
ss.dek: The association plans legal action over traffic police demanding US dollar fines and high license plate fees for commercial vehicles.
paragraphs: The South Sudan Bar Association will sue the Ministry of the Interior and the Traffic Police Department for illegally demanding US dollar fines from private vehicle owners. Stephen Martin Nyichar, Secretary General of the Bar Association, told Radio Tamazuj on Wednesday that the traffic department's fines were not approved by the Ministry of Finance or the Revenue Authority. He stated that requiring citizens to pay fines in US dollars violates directives from the Bank of South Sudan.

Nyichar said the association contacted the Caretaker Interior Minister Lt. Gen. Rizik Zachariah Hassan and informed the Ministry of Justice about the traffic police's unilateral decisions. The Bar Association has given the Ministry of Interior a seven-day deadline to reverse these decisions. An official announcement of the lawsuit will be made at a press conference soon.

The traffic department is also requiring commercial vehicle owners to replace license plates at a cost of USD 400, a move the Bar Association deems illegal as no agreement was reached. These actions occur as South Sudan faces an economic downturn, with widespread financial hardship among the population.

ss.headline: Gunmen kill journalist Veronica Gordon in Western Equatoria ambush
ss.dek: Gordon's killing came as delegates returning from SPLM primaries were ambushed in Miri Loko village, leaving two others wounded, while the attackers' identities and motive remain.
paragraphs: Veronica Lucy Gordon, a veteran journalist and recent parliamentary candidate, and Justin Akim, a former teacher and church elder, were killed on Thursday evening, November 12, when unidentified gunmen attacked a vehicle carrying Sudan People's Liberation Movement (SPLM) delegates on the Lui-Mundri road in Western Equatoria State. The attack occurred at about 7 p.m. in Miri Loko village as the delegates returned from SPLM primaries in Lui Payam to Mundri West. Two other people were wounded, and several delegates fled into nearby bushes.

Eye Radio reported that the attackers targeted the last vehicle in the convoy. Western Equatoria Caretaker Minister of Information Noah Issa told Eye Radio that the identities of the attackers and their motive remain unknown. Gordon, a former South Sudan Broadcasting Corporation (SSBC) journalist, had been nominated to contest a women's seat in the National Legislative Assembly.

The Female Journalists Network (FJN), the Union of Journalists of South Sudan (UJoSS) and the Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) Alliance on Elections condemned the killing in separate statements issued on Friday and called for an urgent investigation and accountability. The CSOs Alliance said violence against women in political life undermines their constitutional rights and equal participation in governance.

ss.headline: Two killed in attack on SPLM delegates in South Sudan
ss.dek: Gunmen ambushed a vehicle carrying ruling party delegates in Western Equatoria State, leaving two dead and others missing.
paragraphs: At least two people were killed and one critically injured when gunmen attacked a vehicle carrying ruling Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM) delegates in Miri Loko village, Western Equatoria State, on Thursday night. The delegates were travelling from Lui Payam to Mundri West County after party primaries and congresses when the ambush occurred around 9 p.m. Several other delegates reportedly fled into nearby bushes during the attack.

Veronica Lucy Gordon, a former journalist nominated for a women’s seat in the National Legislative Assembly, and Justin Akim, a former teacher and elder, were among those killed. The critically injured delegate is receiving treatment at Lui Hospital. Deng Dau Deng, chairperson of the SPLM High-Level Committee in Western Equatoria, confirmed the incident and extended condolences to the families. The state’s Minister of Information, Noah Issah Philip, condemned the violence and urged an end to attacks on roads.

The attack occurred amid SPLM primaries and county congresses ahead of South Sudan’s general elections scheduled for December 22, 2026. Commissioner of Mundri East County, Daite Matthew Bakhieth, confirmed two deaths and other injuries, stating the situation was normal for now. The Western Equatoria State caretaker government expressed concern over the safety of political delegates and road users.

sd.headline: UN food chief urges end to Sudan war amid famine crisis
sd.dek: Hundreds of thousands face starvation as the World Food Programme cuts aid due to funding shortfalls.
paragraphs: Luke J. Lindberg, the new executive director of the United Nations' World Food Programme, has called for an end to the conflict in Sudan, where hundreds of thousands of people are facing famine. Lindberg visited the Goz Al-Salam Camp for Internally Displaced Persons and urged increased financial support for the WFP to expand its humanitarian aid.

The WFP provided food to 4 million people in Sudan during August, but funding constraints forced the organization to cut assistance, leaving 900,000 people without help. The WFP is seeking $520 million to feed 5.4 million people through April 2027.

Sudan's war began in April 2023 between the military and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), creating the world’s largest humanitarian crisis. Approximately 34 million people, nearly two out of every three Sudanese, require assistance, with deadly drone attacks carried out by both rival forces.

sd.headline: Sudanese army retakes key West Kordofan town from RSF
sd.dek: The army and its allied Joint Force announced recapturing Al-Khuway after heavy fighting, seizing territory vital for military and commercial routes.
paragraphs: On Friday, Sudan's army and its allied Joint Force announced they had retaken the strategic town of Al-Khuway in West Kordofan state after heavy fighting with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The Joint Force, an alliance of former Darfur rebel movements fighting alongside the army, said its troops now control Al-Khuway, Sarif Ankoush, Um Labana, Al-Dawdiya and several other areas.

The town sits on road networks that link North and West Kordofan with parts of Darfur. In a statement, Joint Force spokesperson Major Mutwakil Abu Ja said the fighting cost the RSF heavily, including the death of a commander, and claimed 20 RSF combat vehicles were destroyed and 40 seized. Darfur regional governor Minni Arko Minnawi welcomed the recapture, saying the town matters for further military advances and the return of displaced people. The claims could not be independently verified.

The RSF had seized Al-Khuway in May 2025, displacing 2,715 households between May 29 and 30 that year, according to the International Organization for Migration. The army and Joint Force also retook Sarif Ankoush and nearby areas earlier on Friday, and troops are now searching the area and pursuing remaining RSF fighters.

sd.headline: Sudan war financing evades international sanctions
sd.dek: Targeted sanctions by Australia, UK, and UN have failed to stop warring parties from funding their campaigns.
paragraphs: Despite targeted sanctions and travel bans from Australia, the United Kingdom, and a UN Security Council resolution, Sudan's warring factions continue to finance their conflict. Since April 15, 2023, these measures have aimed at commanders, companies, and facilitators, but have not stopped the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) from exploiting resources for private gain and military campaigns.

Research by the Sudan Transparency and Policy Tracker (STPT) indicates that while sanctions have increased costs and disrupted some financial channels, they have not deprived either side of necessary resources or external relationships. Designated businesses, like the SAF-aligned Red Rock Mining Company, have shifted operations through unsanctioned subsidiaries and new commercial relationships, maintaining a global footprint.

Red Rock Mining Company, facing sanctions from the UK, EU, and Switzerland, has leveraged international corporate vehicles to continue operations, boasting a global presence by late 2025. Similarly, the military-affiliated firm Zadna relies on Egypt-based partnerships and domestic dominance to render Western penalties ineffective, securing lucrative contracts without significant blowback, according to STPT.

sd.headline: Sudan's veteran political leader al-Mirghani dies at 90
sd.dek: Mohamed Osman al-Mirghani, leader of the Democratic Unionist Party and head of the Khatmiyya Sufi order, died in Egypt.
paragraphs: Veteran political and religious leader Mohamed Osman al-Mirghani died in Egypt at the age of 90. Al-Mirghani led Sudan’s Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) and headed the influential Khatmiyya Sufi order. Sudan’s Council of Ministers described him as a prominent national and religious figure who significantly contributed to the country’s political life and efforts for unity and consensus.

Al-Mirghani, who drew support from both the DUP and the Khatmiyya Sufi movement, will be buried on Monday at the Sayed Ali Al-Mirghani Mosque in Khartoum North. He inherited leadership of the Khatmiyya order in 1968 and the main DUP faction in 1982. His family has a long history of influence in Sudanese public life.

In November 1988, al-Mirghani met with John Garang, leader of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM), resulting in the Mirghani-Garang Agreement. This peace initiative aimed to end Sudan’s second civil war with a ceasefire and a constitutional conference, but was overtaken by the 1989 military coup.

tg.headline: University of Lomé launches vocational training for students
tg.dek: The University of Lomé's new 'One Student, One Profession' program aims to combat graduate unemployment by offering vocational workshops.
paragraphs: The University of Lomé, led by President Professor Kossivi Hounake, announced the official launch of its "One Student, One Profession" program for the 2026-2027 academic year. This initiative, linked to the government's 2026-2031 roadmap, aims to tackle youth unemployment among graduates and promote entrepreneurship.

However, the program has sparked significant public and academic criticism, with many viewing it as a demeaning intellectual and social downgrade for students. Critics point to overcrowded lecture halls, inadequate teaching equipment, and a shortage of lecturers as pressing issues that need addressing before vocational training is introduced. Students are already struggling to access fundamental knowledge due to these conditions.

The university is proposing workshops in areas like laundry services, soap making, and hairdressing, which critics argue are redundant given existing technical and vocational training centers in Togo. This move is seen by some as a deliberate attempt to lower the ambitions of students, offering them basic subsistence activities as the outcome of higher education.

tg.headline: Japan gives Togo 2.4 billion FCFA for road maintenance training
tg.dek: The funds will equip the regional road maintenance training center with new machinery and enhance its operational capabilities.
paragraphs: Togo will receive 2.4 billion FCFA from Japan to boost the capabilities of the Regional Training Center for Road Maintenance (CERFER). An agreement for the grant, equivalent to 615 million Japanese yen, was signed on November 12 in Lomé. This funding will be used to purchase, transport, and install new equipment at the center to improve its teaching, technical, and operational capacities in road maintenance.

Togo's Minister of Finance and Budget, Georges Essowè Barcola, and Japan's Ambassador to Togo, Gomakubo Junji, signed the documents. Minister Barcola stated the agreement reflects a shared desire to strengthen the partnership through actions addressing priority needs. He highlighted the strategic role of road infrastructure in connecting regions, fostering trade, and improving mobility.

The Japanese ambassador announced a future technical cooperation project for road maintenance capacity building in French-speaking West Africa, including expert secondments and training. JICA's Togo representative, Kato Koichi, described the support as an investment in human resources for future infrastructure development. Japan aims to contribute to local skill development and improve connectivity in Togo and the wider West African sub-region.

tg.headline: Université de Lomé opens maritime institute in Aného
tg.dek: The institute, known as IHES2M, opened on 10 November with 220 students admitted from more than 400 applicants.
paragraphs: The University of Lomé officially opened the Higher Institute of Higher Studies in Maritime Sciences and Professions (IHES2M) on Tuesday, 10 November 2026, in Aného, in the Lacs 1 commune. The institute, formerly the Institute of Maritime Professions (I2M), trains qualified staff for maritime, port, logistics and industrial work.

The ceremony at the Lycée d'Aného-Ville brought together administrative, municipal, university and government officials. The mayor of Lacs 1, Maître Alexis Koffi Aquereburu, pledged to provide land for the institute's future buildings. The institute's director, Professor Bernard Atchrimi, said two professional bachelor's degrees are offered for 2026-2027: port operations and maritime supply chain management, and maritime risks, safety and insurance.

The institute is temporarily housed at the Lycée d'Aného-Ville until its own buildings are constructed. University of Lomé president Professor Kossivi Hounaké said the opening reflects the university's policy of bringing higher education to the regions, and Minister Delegate for Higher Education and Research Professor Gado Tchangbedji called for skills in logistics, security and marine environmental protection.

tg.headline: Algeria loses two more players to injury before Togo match
tg.dek: The Algerian football federation announced on Thursday, November 12, 2026, that Amin Chiakha and Rafik Belghali are out with injuries.
paragraphs: Algeria's national football team, the Greens, will face Togo without two more players due to injuries sustained in training. Amin Chiakha is out with a tibia injury, and Rafik Belghali has a knee injury, forcing them to miss the upcoming Africa Cup of Nations 2027 qualifiers.

The Algerian Football Federation (FAF) officially confirmed the players' unavailability on Thursday, November 12, 2026. Belghali's absence weakens the defensive balance, while Chiakha's injury reduces attacking options for the coach. Saâdi Radouani, a right-back for USM Alger, has been called up to replace Belghali on the right side of the defense.

These latest absences add to a growing list of unavailable players for Algeria. Before Chiakha and Belghali, four other players had already withdrawn from the squad. Bachir Belloumi, an winger for Hull City, is out for an estimated three weeks with a muscle injury, and left-back Jaouen Hadjam has also withdrawn. Midfielder Hicham Boudaoui of Nice was sent back to his club for treatment, with Adem Zorgane called up as his replacement.

tn.headline: Tunisia risks summer power cuts as projects lag
tn.dek: National electricity demand grows 5% annually, requiring 300 MW more power next year.
paragraphs: Tunisia may not finish projects intended to prevent electricity outages by summer 2027, warned Ali Kenzari, president of the national union for photovoltaic equipment installers and maintainers. National electricity demand is increasing by 5% each year, requiring an additional 300 megawatts of capacity next year. Kenzari stated that the timeline for announced projects does not guarantee their completion before summer 2027, risking delays in boosting production capacity.

Kenzari anticipates an electricity deficit that could reach 2,800 MW next year, following a gap of 2,000 to 2,500 MW during last year's peak consumption. He noted that government plans to improve existing power plants, which involve new tenders, might not be implemented until 2028. The government announced measures in early November to increase production before summer 2027, including 300 MW from renewables and 200 MW from gas engines.

As an immediate solution, Kenzari suggested Tunisia increase electricity imports from Algeria, recalling that the current 800 MW exchange agreement was insufficient last year. He also highlighted the potential of solar photovoltaic energy, stating that installed capacity should reach at least 2,500 MW to strengthen national production and reduce reliance on conventional sources.

tn.headline: Tunisia identifies nearly 79,000 undeclared businesses
tn.dek: The finance minister revealed the scale of the informal economy, which accounts for 35.2% of activity.
paragraphs: Tunisia has identified nearly 79,000 economic activities operating without official declaration between 2022 and September 2026. Finance Minister Michket Slama Khaldi announced the figure of 78,688 undeclared activities on Friday before a joint parliamentary session discussing the 2027 state budget. These findings highlight the significant extent of economic operations outside the formal tax system.

The minister stated that the informal economy represents 35.2% of Tunisia's economic activity, a figure that drops to 28.5% when the agricultural sector is excluded. Khaldi emphasized the need to strengthen control mechanisms and inter-agency coordination to address these undeclared operations. In 2025, fiscal interventions generated approximately 7.3 billion dinars in revenue, and a campaign to broaden the tax base and combat evasion is underway.

Fiscal revenues now constitute 91.4% of the state's own resources, a trend attributed to a decline in non-fiscal revenue rather than increased tax pressure. The minister called for intensified efforts to create wealth and diversify state budget funding sources to reduce reliance on debt. A public awareness campaign is also being conducted to encourage formalization.

tn.headline: Tunisian car dealers call for lower duties on imported car parts
tn.dek: The national chamber says eight active car plants face double taxation, and it wants tariffs removed on components used for local assembly.
paragraphs: Ibrahim Debbache, president of the National Chamber of Car Concessionaires and Manufacturers (CNCCA), has asked Parliament's finance committee to cut customs duties on car components imported for assembly in Tunisia. He told Mosaique FM on Friday, November 13, that the measure would encourage local investment and bring new vehicles within reach of ordinary buyers.

Debbache said the duties on components are followed by consumption taxes when the assembled car is sold, which he called a double tax that makes locally built vehicles less competitive. He said the chamber's preferred option is to remove duties entirely on components used in local production, and that the eight plants now operating in the sector are struggling. The proposal was put forward during hearings on the 2027 finance bill.

Debbache also linked the proposal to demand, saying the market needs between 80,000 and 90,000 vehicles a year and that more than 30,000 enter through the parallel market. He argued that cheaper local production could eventually support exports, and he urged that it be built into the "A car for every family" project, which was planned in the 2026 finance law but has not been implemented.

tn.headline: Tunisia loses 0-2 to Libya in CAN 2027 qualifier in Sfax
tn.dek: The Carthage Eagles remain without a win in Group H after a penalty by Ali Youssef and a second goal from Hamdou El Houni.
paragraphs: Tunisia lost 2-0 to Libya on Friday 13 November at the Taïeb Mhiri Stadium in Sfax, in the third round of CAN 2027 qualifying for Group H. Tunisia have still not won in the group, after draws against Uganda (1-1) and Botswana (2-2).

Libya took the lead in the 44th minute, when Ali Youssef converted a penalty awarded after a foul by Ali Maâloul. Hamdou El Houni made it 2-0 from the penalty spot in the 64th minute. Tunisia created several chances in the first half, including a header by Mohamed Dräger in the 23rd minute, but could not score.

Tunisia remain last in Group H with two points, while Libya move level with Uganda at the top on four points, though Uganda have played two matches to Libya's three. Uganda play Botswana on Saturday 14 November. The return match against Libya is scheduled for Tuesday 17 November.

tn.headline: Tunisian olive oil expert joins jury at Buenos Aires competition
tn.dek: Professor Imene Trabelsi Trigui, a Tunisian specialist in olive oil, is serving as a jury member at the fifth Buenos Aires International Olive Oil Competition, which brings.
paragraphs: Professor Imene Trabelsi Trigui, a Tunisian specialist in olive oil, was due to sit on the jury of the fifth Buenos Aires International Olive Oil Competition (BAIOOC) on November 13 and 14, 2026, in Argentina's capital. The competition has been held there since 2021 and aims to promote the quality of extra virgin olive oil.

The Argentine Embassy in Tunisia congratulated Trabelsi Trigui in a statement, saying it was pleased that a Tunisian expert would bring her knowledge and experience to an event held in Argentina. The embassy said she would show the know-how, tradition and excellence of Tunisian olive growing.

The embassy described the appointment as a chance to celebrate ties between Argentina and Tunisia, two countries that share a love of the olive tree. Local outlet Webdo reported the same appointment, describing Trabelsi Trigui as an ambassador for Tunisian olive oil in Argentina.

zm.headline: Hichilema orders urban teachers moved to rural schools
zm.dek: Public workers who fail to return to their original posts could lose their government salaries, the president has warned.
paragraphs: President Hakainde Hichilema has ordered that surplus teachers in towns and cities be moved at once to rural schools that are short of staff. The same order covers nurses under the Ministry of Health and agricultural extension officers who have left their assigned posts.
Those who do not go back to the stations they were first posted to could be struck off the government payroll, the president said. The aim is to fill gaps in rural areas where staff are missing.
The report gives no timetable for the moves and does not say when the affected workers must report to their new postings.

zm.headline: Zambia police to go digital
zm.dek: Government plans to deploy surveillance cameras to improve crime prevention and detection.
paragraphs: The Zambian government plans to digitalise police operations to enhance crime prevention, detection, and national security. Minister of Home Affairs and Internal Security Clement Andeleki announced the initiative, which will involve installing surveillance cameras in public areas. These cameras are intended to enable the police to respond more effectively to criminal activities across the country.

Dr. Andeleki stated that the deployment of these cameras is a strategic move to strengthen the Zambia Police Service's capabilities. The aim is to create a more robust system for monitoring public spaces and gathering evidence. This digital transformation is expected to improve the overall efficiency of law enforcement in combating crime.

The initiative is part of a broader effort to modernise the police force and adapt to new technological approaches in security. The government believes this digital upgrade will significantly contribute to maintaining public order and safety throughout Zambia.

zm.headline: Mulendema communal reservoir gives Zambian farmers water beyond the rainy season
zm.dek: A communal reservoir in Chief Mulendema's area, Mumbwa district, is designed to hold about 1.62 million litres of water for smallholder farmers.
paragraphs: A communal reservoir built through the Water and Soil Accelerator (WASA) project is giving smallholder farmers in Chief Mulendema's area of Mumbwa district, Central Province, a way to farm through dry spells. The reservoir can provide an estimated 1.62 million litres of water every five to six weeks with its current pump installation.

The Mini Water Reservoir supports 50 households, or 250 end-users, in the Nalusanga GMA. Solidaridad Southern Africa, backed by the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), is running the project with GreenCare Eco Solutions, Zambia's Ministry of Agriculture, the Water Resources Management Authority (WARMA) and traditional leaders. Sheila Garakara, Solidaridad's Country Manager for Zambia, said the reservoir widens farmers' choices, particularly for women growing food.

Community members, particularly women and young people, have received compost and fertiliser, and a vegetable garden is planned for later this year. IWMI's gender researcher, Dr Ojong Enokenwa Baa, said women and young people must help set the rules for managing the reservoir, and that a women's club provides an important foundation, though more support is needed.

eh.headline: Sahrawi PM accuses Spain of backing Moroccan autonomy plan
eh.dek: Bucharaya Hamudi Beyun says the Polisario Front will use legal, warlike and non-warlike means to defend Sahrawi rights, ahead of the 50th EUCOCO in Madrid.
paragraphs: Sahrawi Prime Minister Bucharaya Hamudi Beyun accused the Spanish government of Pedro Sánchez of backing Morocco's autonomy plan for Western Sahara, alongside the United States. Speaking on Friday at a press conference in Madrid before the 50th EUCOCO, he said the Polisario Front is ready to use "all legal, warlike and non-warlike instruments" to defend Sahrawi rights.

Beyun compared Sánchez's position to that of the last Franco government, calling it inexplicable that a socialist government now takes the stance a Franco government once did. He said Morocco and its Western allies sought a Security Council resolution making autonomy "the only solution" and turning the MINURSO mission into a cheap one, and that Russia vetoed it. Spain is not on the Council but sits in the Group of Friends of Western Sahara, which prepares resolutions on the territory.

Beyun said Morocco is moving and concentrating troops along the wall, probably to step up military action, and blamed the Americans, Spain, France and the United Kingdom for the policy. Asked whether Morocco was provoking escalation, he pointed to the 1991 ceasefire, which he said Rabat accepted because it could no longer sustain the war. The conflict has run six years since the ceasefire broke down at Guerguerat.

Sahrawi Prime Minister Bucharaya Hamudi Beyun accused the Spanish government of Pedro Sánchez of backing Morocco's autonomy plan for Western Sahara, alongside the United States. Speaking on Friday at a press conference in Madrid before the 50th EUCOCO, he said the Polisario Front is ready to use "all legal, warlike and non-warlike instruments" to defend Sahrawi rights.

Beyun compared Sánchez's position to that of the last Franco government, calling it inexplicable that a socialist government now takes the stance a Franco government once did. He said Morocco and its Western allies sought a Security Council resolution making autonomy "the only solution" and turning the MINURSO mission into a cheap one, and that Russia vetoed it. Spain is not on the Council but sits in the Group of Friends of Western Sahara, which prepares resolutions on the territory.

Beyun said Morocco is moving and concentrating troops along the wall, probably to step up military action, and blamed the Americans, Spain, France and the United Kingdom for the policy. Asked whether Morocco was provoking escalation, he pointed to the 1991 ceasefire, which he said Rabat accepted because it could no longer sustain the war. The conflict has run six years since the ceasefire broke down at Guerguerat.
eh.why: Spain's support for autonomy, if it continues, would weaken the UN mission that monitors the territory and shift the Security Council's terms for any future deal.

ls.headline: World Vision unveils five-year plan for 650,000 vulnerable Lesotho children
ls.dek: The 'BOLD HOPE' National Strategy 2026-2030 covers children from early childhood to adolescence, with work on health, nutrition and child protection.
paragraphs: World Vision International Lesotho launched its 'BOLD HOPE' National Strategy 2026-2030 last Friday, aimed at improving the wellbeing of 650,000 vulnerable children from early childhood to adolescence.

National Director James Chifwelu said the launch reaffirmed the charity's commitment to letting every child in Lesotho live life in its fullness, whatever their circumstances. The strategy promises agile, low-cost, high-impact programmes.

World Vision has worked in Lesotho since 1987 across six Area Development Programmes, and Chifwelu cited progress on child protection systems, water, sanitation and hygiene, and menstrual health, which led to a National Menstrual Health Strategy.

ls.headline: Lesotho ranks 16th of 54 in African governance index
ls.dek: The country scored 58.3 out of 100, above both the African and Southern African averages, in the 2026 Ibrahim Index.
paragraphs: Lesotho has placed 16th out of 54 African countries in the 2026 Ibrahim Index of African Governance, scoring 58.3 out of 100. The Mo Ibrahim Foundation released the index on October 31, covering governance from 2016 to 2025. Lesotho's score is above the African average of 50.1 and the Southern African regional average of 56.1, a gain of 1.9 points over the decade.

The index grades four areas: security and rule of law, participation, rights and inclusion, economic opportunity, and human development. Lesotho scored highest on participation and rights, and every area improved over the period. The country scored 100 on the absence of armed conflict, laws against violence toward women, and civil registration.

The index also flags weak spots. The transport network scored just 16.8, and public perception of economic opportunity stood at 18.8. Law enforcement fell 33.7 points to 25.8, and perceptions of anti-corruption dropped 21.5 points.
